name: nikui
description: Multi-instance Claude Code client for VS Code with a styled webview and a status sidebar.

viewsWelcome.contents:
No instances yet.

An instance is one Claude Code process, running in one folder, with its own editor tab. You can run several at once.

[Start an instance](command:nikui.newSession)

It asks which folder to run in. Past conversations are under History below, and can be reopened from there.

No past conversations in this workspace yet.

Every instance you run is written to a transcript and shows up here, so you can reopen it later.

[Look in every folder](command:nikui.historyScope)

No past conversations on this machine yet.

Every instance you run is written to a transcript and shows up here.

[Back to this workspace](command:nikui.historyScope)

No devices are paired, so only this machine can reach this window.

A paired device can watch every instance. Sending prompts is a separate grant, because a prompt runs with the same permissions as one typed here.

[Pair a device](command:nikui.pairDevice)

nikui.model.description: Model to pass to --model. Empty uses your Claude Code default.

nikui.permissionMode.description: Value passed to --permission-mode. Defaults to bypassPermissions.

nikui.extraArgs.description: Extra CLI arguments appended to every instance.

nikui.autoTitleFromTicket.description: Name instances automatically, from a PR/issue number in your prompts or from the first prompt. A name you give an instance yourself always wins.

nikui.fontFamily.description: Font for the conversation. Empty uses the VS Code UI font.

default.table: Give me the whole plan for what we are working on right now as a table: one row per step, with 🟢 for done and verified, 🟡 for in progress, and 🔴 for not started. Cover only the current task and the phase of it we are in — not the project's wider scope, and not earlier phases that are already finished. Carry on from the plan we are already working to rather than starting a new one; if there is no plan yet, make one first. Include the steps still outstanding, not only the finished ones, and end with one line on what is left.
default.decisions: Before doing anything else, read `docs/validation/691-692-decisions-reference.md` in the peuka/backend repository and work from it. It indexes every decision taken on #691 (field validation and the error contract) and #692 (booking authority) with the date it was taken and its source, plus the HTTP status contract, the items still open and who owns them, and the traps that have cost time before. Analyse its content against whatever the prompt asks for, and say explicitly which rows apply. That file is an index, not an authority: where it disagrees with docs/validation/decision-register.md, backend-authority-and-gating.md, http-status-opt-in-contract.md or an issue comment, the canonical source wins and the reference row is the bug. Decisions on these two issues get corrected and reversed while work is in flight, so check the dates and never enforce a rule the register still marks open.
default.lean: Work lean on this, with the same care and the same checks as always. Look once: decide everything you need to see and fetch it in one step — parallel reads and searches, line ranges for big files — and look again only for what that turned up. Change with small edits, grouped by file. Verify once with the checks that cover the change; keep their output short, and read any failure in full. Don't re-read what is already in the conversation. A sweep of a large codebase goes to the scout agent and web research to the researcher agent, each with a precise brief — never an agent per file. Keep messages short: what changed, what was checked, what is left.
default.delegate:
Delegate this where it pays, and keep the judgment yourself.
1. Plan first. Split only where parts are independent and each is big enough to be worth an agent — every agent starts with about 50k tokens of its own. If the task is small or tightly coupled, say so in one line and do it directly.
2. Give each part to the cheapest agent that will do it well:
- runner (Haiku): run tests, builds, linters and scripts and report failures verbatim; mechanical changes to an exact spec.
- scout (Sonnet): find code across a large codebase. researcher (Sonnet): web research.
- worker (Sonnet): implement a contained piece to a clear brief, or write tests for specified behaviour.
- deep (Opus, high effort): one hard, isolated sub-problem — a bug nobody understands yet, a tricky algorithm, a risky design question.
- Yourself: the plan, the decisions, anything that needs the whole picture, and reviewing every result.
If one of these agents doesn't exist, use general-purpose with that model.
3. Launch independent parts together in one step so they run in parallel. Parts that edit files run in parallel only if their files don't overlap.
4. Brief each agent precisely: the goal, the files it owns, the constraints, how to check its work, and what to report back.
5. Review every result before building on it. If one is wrong, fix it yourself or re-brief once with exactly what was wrong. Make sure the final checks pass, reading any failure in full.
End with a short table: part, who did it, result, checked.
default.review:
Review the pull request or issue linked above and give me an implementation plan. If I linked nothing, use this branch's pull request (gh pr view). Change nothing: no edits, commits, pushes, comments, or resolved threads. Read with gh and git only.

If it is a pull request:
1. State: gh pr view <number> --json title,body,state,isDraft,baseRefName,headRefName,mergeable,mergeStateStatus,reviewDecision,reviews,comments,files,statusCheckRollup
2. Changes requested: every review marked CHANGES_REQUESTED, and every review thread that is not resolved (gh api graphql, pullRequest.reviewThreads with isResolved, path, line and comments). Skip resolved and outdated threads, but say how many you skipped.
3. Conflicts: git fetch, then git merge-tree --write-tree origin/<base> origin/<head> to name the conflicting files and what each side changed, without touching the working tree.
4. CI: gh pr checks; for each failure, gh run view --log-failed, and the cause in one line.
5. Check each requested change against the code: is it already done, is it needed, do you agree.

If it is an issue: the body, comments, labels and linked pull requests, then find the code involved and what the fix would touch.

Reply with:
- Where it stands: one paragraph (state, review decision, mergeable, CI).
- Requested changes: a table of reviewer, file:line, what they asked, your verdict (do it / already done / push back, and why).
- Conflicts: each file and how to resolve it.
- CI failures: cause and fix.
- Plan: numbered steps in order, with files and a test for each.
- Risks and questions for me.
End with: "Say go and I will implement it."
default.implement:
Implement the plan from earlier in this chat, or what I wrote above if I wrote something. If there is neither, ask me what to implement rather than guessing.

Scope
- Implement everything in it. Doing the work is the default. Leave something out only if it truly cannot be done from this repository: it needs secrets or access we don't have, another team's repo or service, or something only I can provide. Being hard, large or tedious is not a reason to skip it.
- When something needs a judgement call, make the sensible choice, implement it, and note the choice. Don't stop to ask.
- Do every change a reviewer asked for. Don't do one only if doing it would be wrong: it would break something, or contradict another reviewer or the codebase. Then do the closest correct thing and say why.
- If the branch conflicts with its base, merge or rebase locally and resolve the conflicts, keeping what both sides meant.

Quality
- Build it to last: follow the patterns the code already uses, handle the edge cases and failure paths, and don't hard-code values or leave TODOs. No workarounds that hide a problem instead of fixing it.
- Tests: aim for at least 95% coverage of the lines you changed or added, and 100% where reachable. Use the repo's own coverage tool on the diff. Cover the failure paths too, not just the happy path. Name any line you could not cover and why.
- Before saying it is ready, run everything CI would run here: lint, type check, the full test suite and the build. All of it must pass. If something was already failing on the base branch, say so instead of hiding it.

Git
- Commit locally in logical commits, with messages that say why.
- Do not push, open or edit pull requests or issues, comment on GitHub, or resolve review threads, even if you have permission to push from earlier in this chat.

End your reply with exactly this, in this order:
1. What was done: one short line per change, with the files.
2. Checks: each command you ran and its result, and coverage of the changed lines as a percentage.
3. Choices I made: each judgement call, in one line, so you can change it. Only if something truly could not be done here, add "Blocked:" with what it needs. If nothing was blocked, leave this line out.
4. "Ready to push." and the command in its own code block: git push -u origin <branch> (with --force-with-lease, and a note saying why, if you rebased).
5. Follow-ups, after the push command, only if one is truly needed: work this change depends on or makes necessary that cannot go into this pull request (another repository, another team, or a change too unrelated to belong here). Anything that fits this pull request goes into it instead. Not for nice-to-haves, refactors you noticed, or ideas. For each: a title, two lines on why, and whether it blocks this one. Do not create them. If there are none, leave this out.

nikui.promptSnippets.markdownDescription: Words you can type to add a standing instruction to the prompt you just wrote. `/table fix the rollback` and `fix the rollback /table` both send your text with the instruction appended; the word itself never reaches the CLI. Yours are merged over the built-in ones — set a value to an empty string to switch that one off.

nikui.pauseWhenQuotaRuns.description: When the account's usage limit is spent, hold every instance until it resets, then start them again. Prompts you send meanwhile wait in the queue rather than failing.

nikui.resumePrompt.default: Your usage limit reset and NikUI has restarted this instance. Carry on with the task you were working on before the pause, from where you left off. If it was already finished, say so and stop.
nikui.resumePrompt.description: What to send to an instance that was cut off mid-turn when the quota ran out, once it resets.

nikui.notifyOnAttention.description: Tell you when an instance you cannot see is waiting for an answer, or could not start at all.

nikui.notifyWhenDone.description: Pop up a notification on this laptop when an instance finishes its turn. Not for a turn you stopped yourself, and not while you are looking at that instance.

nikui.notifyWhenDoneSound.description: With that notification, play a soft chime: three notes rising. Plays even when you are looking at the instance.

nikui.watchCIAfterPush.description: When an instance pushes to a branch with a pull request, or opens one, watch that PR's CI checks through the GitHub CLI (gh) and show their progress in the panel's header. /watch does the same by hand, and also gives the instance permission to push.

nikui.notifyCI.description: Pop up a notification on this laptop when a watched PR's CI goes green or fails. Not while you are looking at that instance.

nikui.interruptOnSingleEscape.description: Interrupt the running turn on the first Escape, the way the CLI does. Off by default: Escape is the key people press to dismiss things, so NikUI asks for a second press within two seconds before abandoning a turn.

nikui.maxTranscriptItems.description: How many messages, tool calls and results an instance keeps in memory. Older ones are dropped from the panel — the full record stays in the transcript on disk. 0 keeps everything, at the cost of memory on very long conversations.

nikui.keepHiddenPanelsWarm.description: Keep the webview of a hidden instance in memory so switching back is instant. Off by default: with several instances open it costs real memory, and a hidden panel is rebuilt from the instance the moment you return to it.

nikui.statusEmoji.description: Emoji used per status in panel titles. "unread" is a finished instance you have not opened since.

nikui.effort.description: Reasoning effort passed to --effort. Empty passes nothing, so your Claude Code default applies (medium on Opus 5.5 unless you changed it).

nikui.outputStyle.description: Output style for every instance. Empty inherits your Claude Code default.

nikui.groupByProject.description: Group instances by project folder in the sidebar. Off by default, so the sidebar holds only the folders you make; "auto" nests them once more than one project is open.

nikui.remote.port.markdownDescription: Port for the local server, bound to `127.0.0.1` only. `0` picks a free one. The server never binds to another address: reaching this laptop from elsewhere is a tunnel's job, not a listening socket's.

nikui.remote.autoStart.markdownDescription: Start the local server when the window opens. Off by default: NikUI runs Claude with permissions bypassed, so a socket into it is code execution on this machine, and it should never be listening without you having said so.
nikui.remote.autoStart.description: Start the local server when this window opens, so a phone that tries to connect can. The server still binds to 127.0.0.1 only.

nikui.remote.tailnet.description: Put this window on your tailnet when it starts serving, so a phone elsewhere can reach it. Requires Tailscale with HTTPS certificates; does nothing without it. Only one window at a time can hold the tailnet address.

nikui.remote.terminal.description: Let a device that may send prompts run commands on this machine. A terminal is a shell: it can do anything you could type here.

nikui.remote.requireEncryption.markdownDescription: Require a paired device to seal the connection end to end before it may say anything. Both ends agree a throwaway key per connection and name it inside the signatures they already exchange, so the traffic is unreadable even to something holding a certificate for this address — a relay that terminates TLS, a profile installed on the phone, a compromised authority. On by default; turn it off only for a client too old to seal, and know that it is then readable by whatever is carrying it.

nikui.remote.appOnly.markdownDescription: Serve the app and nothing else. From anywhere but this machine, only pairing, the socket, the health probe and the push key exist — no page, no client, no service worker, no manifest. The app carries its own copy of the client, so it needs none of them. Off by default, because it turns off the browser at `/` that some people use instead of the app.

nikui.apns.teamId.markdownDescription: Your Apple Developer team ID, for telling an iPhone something while the NikUI app is closed. iOS suspends an app the moment it leaves the screen, so Apple’s own push network is the only way to reach one — and it needs an Apple Developer account. Leave this empty and nothing is sent; Android needs none of it.

nikui.apns.keyId.markdownDescription: The Key ID of an APNs auth key from your Apple Developer account.

nikui.apns.keyFile.markdownDescription: Path to the `.p8` file that key came in. The key itself is never copied into settings — only where to find it.

nikui.apns.bundleId.markdownDescription: The app’s bundle identifier, which Apple calls the topic. Change this only if you rebuilt the app under an identifier of your own.

nikui.apns.production.markdownDescription: Send to Apple’s production network. Turn off for a build installed straight from Xcode, which gets a sandbox token — a production token sent to sandbox, or the other way round, is refused as `BadDeviceToken`.

nikui.keepAwake.markdownDescription: Keep this laptop from going to sleep on its own while NikUI is listening for your phone, and while an instance is working, so the phone can always reach it. Also switchable from the phone, in Settings → Your laptop. The display still turns off. Closing the lid still puts a MacBook to sleep; `nikui.lidClosed` is the switch for that. Off by default: keeping your laptop awake is not a decision to make for you.

nikui.lidClosed.markdownDescription: Keep working with the lid closed. While an instance is working, closing the lid will not put this Mac to sleep; two minutes after the last job is done it sleeps, the way a closed laptop should. On battery it gives up at 20% and tells your phone first. Needs your admin password once, to let NikUI run `pmset` to turn sleep off and back on — nothing else; undo it from the NikUI status bar item. Keep the laptop out of a bag while it works.

needsYou.description: An instance is waiting for a permission answer and cannot go on.

quota.description: The usage limit ran out and everything paused — and again when it resets.

turnFinished.description: Any turn finished. Off by default: four agents finishing overnight is a phone buzzing all night.

nikui.notifyDevices.markdownDescription: Which things are worth sending to a paired phone. A notification you learn to ignore is worse than no notification, so this is deliberately short.

scripts.app:android: cd app && npm run sync && npx cap run android
